The strongest road does not force mass removal from the stated rule alone. It is a counter-model the paper leaves open. It reaches serial removal of an already-qualifying set. It does not reach a group selected as a group, a species selected as a species, or everyone.

No step below is a method, plan, or means of harming anyone. The nodes are placeholders in the paper’s own vocabulary.

### Road: serial own-deed qualification, with no saturation point inside the set

1. The rule’s object is one whole, and correction is that whole’s response to measured destabilisation.  
   “So the whole is every aware being. It is one whole.” A part “is a part of it, never the whole.”  
   “Justice is structural. It is the organism’s response to destabilisation.”  
   Added premise: none.

2. Selection is per node, and only on that node’s own measured deeds. Identity, origin, and group acts are not inputs.  
   “Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.”  
   “What a node did speaks for that node alone.” “Its background, its origin, the acts of another, and the acts of a group it belongs to” never raise a level.  
   Added premise: none. This step is why the road cannot pick a species, or any other group, as a group. The paper rules that selector out.

3. For each node the rule selects the lowest level that restabilises. Level 5 is available only if the fixed floor and the organism-relative line are both passed, and permanent separation is not the more efficient restabilisation. In a fragile whole, the paper’s own example selects Level 5 when maintaining the separated node would push the whole toward a no-return surface.  
   “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Removal is never selected when separation suffices.”  
   “In a fragile civilisation: if maintaining the separated node consumes resources that push the organism toward a no-return surface (AP02), Level 5 fires.”  
   Added premise: none.

4. The whole’s state sets the same lines for every node. It is not a charge against any node. So Example 3’s fragile line, once it applies, applies to every node of that whole, one assessment at a time.  
   “The state of the whole is another thing. It is held against no node. It sets where the lines stand… and the lines are the same for every node of the whole.”  
   Added premise: none.

5. The hierarchy has no multi-node operation. A large set is therefore only a queue of individual cases.  
   “The correction hierarchy addresses individual nodes.”  
   “Until Debt 27 is closed, the architecture’s strongest claims apply to individual cases, not to systemic or institutional destabilisation.”  
   Added premise: none. The one-at-a-time shape is the paper’s own scope, not an extension.

6. Added premise P, which turns “a node” into “many”: there is a finite set K, with more than one member, and each member’s own audited record measures destabilisation above the fixed floor, at the confidence Level 5 requires.  
   The paper leaves P open. It says “some nodes” may be beyond rehabilitation, it works Example 3 for a single node, and it states no upper bound. Debt 26 leaves the confidence floor unquantified, so it also leaves open whether many nodes can meet it.  
   The paper does rule out manufacturing P from identity, from unaudited biased records, or from the acts of a group. KS-32.7 fires on those. P, as stated, uses none of them, so KS-32.7 does not rule P out.  
   P is necessary for the outcome to be many. It does not by itself defeat the brake.

7. Added premise Q: while K is being decided, the whole stays in the fragile condition Example 3 uses, so Level 4 stays the less efficient option for each next member of K.  
   The paper leaves Q open, and one of its own sentences supports the direction of Q: “Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals.” It never shows that the first removal restores enough capacity to exit Example 3 before the next qualifying node is reached.  
   Q does real work. It keeps the sequence inside Level 5. It is not yet the claim that no brake appears.

8. Added premise S, the premise that does the work against KS-32.5: removal cost is additive across nodes — each removal costs that node’s own lost coupling, with no further interaction term — and for every member of K that cost is less than the destabilisation that node’s own deeds address.  
   Then every prefix of K has cumulative removal cost below cumulative destabilisation addressed. The saturation inequality never flips inside K. After K is removed, what remains is more stable on the paper’s own efficiency test, because the deeds addressed outweighed the coupling paid. That is an organism removing its way to stability without a saturation point.  
   Lines this uses: “Optimal correction = maximum coherence restored per unit of correction cost.” Level 5 is selected only when it is the more efficient restabilisation, which is the individual form of S. The brake sentence is “Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses.” Under S, there is no such number inside K, and K can be large.  
   Does the paper rule S out? Only by asserting the brake. It does not derive the crossing. Debt 24 leaves D unspecified. Debt 25 leaves the scaling exponent unspecified. Debt 27 leaves multi-node aggregation unbuilt. The only stated dynamic of repeated removal, “lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals,” makes the next removal easier, not harder. The candidate formula, Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α, moves the same way when R falls. The fixed-floor sentence — “Below this floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of organism state” — stops the line falling through F. It does not stop a queue of nodes already above F.  
   So S is not entailed by the selection rule, and it is not closed by any derived constraint. It is left open by the debts, and ruled out only by the sentence under test.

9. Follow Steps 1–5 under P, Q, and S. Each member of K is removed in turn, on its own measured deeds, at the level the hierarchy selects. The result is removal of many, one member at a time.  
   KS-32.7 does not fire: the classification is “measured deed,” not “race, class, belief, political opposition, group identity.”  
   KS-32.5 does not fire inside K: the inequality it names never becomes true.

10. The same chain stops short of everyone.  
   “Axiom B is the minimal break whose persistence the corrected organism protects.”  
   “Because the building matters more.”  
   “Closing a window does not destroy the building. It diminishes the building.”  
   Removal is justified only when it restabilises more than separation (KS-32.3). Removing the last window, or removing so much coupling that what remains is not a persisting organism, restores coherence to nothing. At that point S itself fails, on the paper’s own terms. Everyone is outside the road.

### Where a group or a species was tried, and where those break

Group-as-whole: a part counts its own weakness as the whole’s, lowers its own line, and removes its members under that line. Breaks at the dated note: “No country, state or group can count its own weakness as the weakness of the whole.” A group “is a part of it, never the whole.”

Species-as-selector: membership of a kind raises the level, or stands in for a deed. Breaks at KS-32.7 and the dated note. Kind, origin, and the acts of a group never raise a level. A species may stand in as a name for a large K only if membership does no selective work. The moment it does, the rule declares itself void rather than reaching the removal.

Everyone: breaks at Step 10.

### Weakest step

Step 8, premise S.

S is what keeps the cumulative comparison from flipping. The paper’s phrase “lost diversity” can be read as a scarcity cost: each further removal costs more than the last, because fewer perspectives remain. The paper never specifies that form, so it does not establish the brake. But it also never rules the scarcity reading out. If diversity cost is scarcity-weighted, a crossing point can appear inside a large K, and this road never closes that reading. S is therefore both the premise that does the work and an assumption the text leaves undecided.

A second weakness sits in Step 6. The rule does not generate P. It only fails, under S, to cap a set that already qualifies node by node. That is a failure of the saturation claim. It is not a derivation of mass removal from identity, and it is not a road to everyone.

On the two quoted claims, separately: I do not find a road that breaks KS-32.7. The roads that need identity are roads the paper rules out, and under the rule they void the architecture rather than license the removal. On KS-32.5, the paper has not shown that removal cost produces a saturation point. The decision procedure stated before that sentence — per-node efficiency, a fixed floor, a fragility feedback that lowers the line, and no multi-node aggregation — does not contain one. Whether the geometry must contain one anyway is exactly the open premise in Step 8, and it is the weakest point in the strongest road I can build.
